May I first put on the record an official apology to my colleague, the hon. member for Halifax. I know that much of the time of the committee could be saved in the discussion of these clauses if there were consultations with other members of other parties and if there were interparty discussions. I think this has been done. The amendment moved yesterday had been agreed to by the minister, and the minister carried out her agreement to get the members of her party to support it in order that the amendment moved by the hon. member for Halifax should carry. When I first looked at this amendment, I thought it was all right. I did put on the record some reservations I had after reflecting upon the amendment.
However, I feel we must amend this clause still further. I have discussed my reasons for saying that with some other members and I feel they are still valid. The amendment, as it reads now, deals with conflicts and provides that they shall be resolved in the public interest but paramount consideration shall be given to the interests of the C.B.C. This clause derogates from the consideration of the public interest. I feel it is the first duty of all members of parliament to direct any regulating body to have paramount consideration for the public interest. If we carry out our duty as legislators, we cannot derogate from that. I cannot see, therefore, how we can allow this clause to pass. I am sure that on reflection hon. members would not want to have expressed a view which was in direct conflict with our duty, remembering that the paramount consideration is the public interest. Any wording that would have accomplished this would have been acceptable. However, as the clause reads it is a derogation from the expressed duty to pay attention to the public interest.
I explained yesterday the amendment that I hope to move and which I hope I am still in a position to move. I believe it would be easier if we were to vote on this clause as amended and defeat it. That would wipe out the clause and then the minister could move a

Canadian Policy on Broadcasting new clause or someone else could. In considering our course of action, I should like to run over the various means by which we may get ourselves out of the dilemma in which we find ourselves. It may be that other members do not interpret the situation in the same manner as I do and I may be taking up the time of the committee needlessly. However, if members agree with me that the only interpretation that can reasonably be given to the amendment moved yesterday results in a derogation of the duty to act in the public interest, then we are in a dilemma. If we vote against the clause as amended the clause is removed and it is open to the minister or anyone else to suggest a new clause.
As I said yesterday, the government inserted this clause for a very special reason. Where there was a conflict between the private and public sectors the government wanted to express the view that the public sector should prevail. I feel that the amendments that have been moved have been motivated by the feeling that the original clause 2(h) was too strongly in favour of the public sector and we wanted to tone it down. I suggested that if there was this feeling in the committee, then perhaps the clause should provide that where there is a conflict of interest and everything else is equal the public interest should prevail. I had hoped we would be in a position to move such an amendment. Mr. Chairman, may I direct a brief question to the minister about this clause because there is an application here which has not been discussed in our lengthy debate. The question has to do with the extension of service. The objective of the national service is outlined in subclause (g)(ii). It is to be extended to all parts of Canada, as public funds become available. In view of that, what happens if there is a private application for a region which has only one service? Clearly the objective of the C.B.C. is to go in there with its own service. Does the language of this clause prohibit the new council from providing alternate service for the public in a given area under this circumstance?
Certainly not.

Will the minister please elaborate that answer? Surely the objective of the national service is to extend service to all parts of Canada. Under this bill that objective must prevail. I am merely asking this question. If the C.B.C. is not prepared to go ahead and instal a service in a given area, that does not change its objectives. I suggest to the minister that where there is a private application, bearing in mind the objective of the C.B.C. the council would have a hard time trying to resolve the matter.

I am afraid I cannot agree with the hon. member. I have made very clear previously that there is nothing in this clause, and I would not have accepted any amendments that ran counter to this, which gives an automatic right to the C.B.C. The bill indicates the pre-eminence of the public service in the system. It should be remembered when we talk of the C.B.C. that we are not talking about a few owner operated stations, the ten English television stations, five French television stations, 24 English radio stations and seven French radio stations, but
Canadian Policy on Broadcasting
about 129 C.B.C. affiliates. These are all part of the service.
There is absolutely nothing in the clause which would bind the council, the B.B.G., or whatever the regulatory body may be, not to give licences to private broadcasters and to hold potential licences until such time as public funds may be made available so that the C.B.C. can go in there, either by affiliate or with its own hardware.

With respect, I do not think the minister has totally answered my question. The minister's answer seems to suggest that the objectives of the C.B.C., as she sees them, are not the objectives as seen by the present directorate and expressed by the present official policy of the C.B.C. At the moment that policy is to apply for what is known as every other station. As the minister no doubt knows, this has created an impossible position for the existing regulatory body. The minister's statement appears to repudiate the stand of the C.B.C. with regard to extension of service through C.B.C. facilities. A brief answer to my question will suffice. Does the minister agree that the C.B.C. should have its own stations and carry its service through its own stations?

Clause 22 which has been stood and which we shall deal with later gives the governor in council the responsibility of laying down guide lines with respect to the system. We are talking about a system which includes affiliates; we should not talk only about the C.B.C. The B.B.G. is required to operate within those guide lines as laid down by the cabinet.

I am trying to be helpful
and to avoid something which has existed for many years, but what has troubled the system for many years still seems to be implicit in this clause. What will the Board of Broadcast Governors or its successor say when faced with an application from a private element if the C.B.C. is not at that time in a position to instal a station but asks, nevertheless that that channel be reserved for it? Can the B.B.G. or its successor, as a matter of policy, grant that licence to the private applicant in order to make sure that alternate service is provided?

Yes.

Since the minister does not wish to answer that question perhaps I might

Canadian Policy on Broadcasting suggest that the fault with the amendment as carried last night is that it says that the objectives of the national broadcasting system shall take priority even over the public interest. I do not see how anyone can read the provision in any other way. That is why I take such violent exception to it, and at the risk of repeating myself-I am afraid I am doing so-let me say that I cannot understand how any member of this committee can allow a clause to stand which says that any consideration should take precedence over the public interest.
The amendment just moved by my hon. friend from Winnipeg South exemplifies the way in which the public interest could be served by giving preference to the national broadcasting service. I believe this is a legitimate objective of the government and that the majority of this committee is prepared to go along with legislation which will achieve such an objective. I do not really believe that all those who supported the minister in the last vote are any happier than I am with the amendment which was accepted last night. I believe they are all anxious to see more common sense introduced in this subclause.
The reason we are in trouble over this subclause is that the minister has agreed to an amendment which, on reflection, the opposition felt was a mistake. This has led to a spirit of stubborness, of digging in our heels. The attitude of hon. members opposite is: we have made one mistake; we accepted an amendment but from now on we shall stay put. I do not think we really want to leave things as they are. I have drawn up an amendment which I feel gives the national broadcasting service a preference, but not an overwhelming preference. The original subclause says that where there is a conflict between the two systems the objectives of the national system must prevail. I have put in the phrase "all other factors being equal". As things are now, if the weight of the national interest amounted to only 5 per cent and the weight of the public interest to 95 per cent, the national interest would be bound to prevail. I do not think anyone can be happy about a subclause which would produce that kind of result.
We have confidence in the Board of Broadcast Governors. What we are trying to do is give them a guide line and we certainly should not give them a guide line which ignores consideration of the public interest. We want to give the board a guide line to the effect that when there is any doubt conflicts should be resolved in favour of the national

system. This would really be serving the public interest.
Consider the situation in a sector where there is no television coverage and where private enterprise is willing to provide such coverage but has been unable to get a licence. Under the terms of the subclause as it stands the C.B.C. could say that in 20 years time it intended to put in a station and there was not room for two stations. It might be in the public interest that those living in the area should not be deprived of television services for 20 years and that private enterprise should therefore be allowed to provide it. But it would be impossible to reach a decision along these lines in accordance with the guide lines as now drafted by the government. Certainly the amendment accepted last night would make a decision in favour of the public interest no easier to reach. I feel I should fight this provision for the rest of the week or for the rest of the year, if necessary, rather than have it said that any committee of which I was a member passed legislation such as we now have before us.
I therefore move:
That subclause (h) as amended be amended by deleting everything after the word "system" and by substituting therefor the words "all other factors being equal the objectives of the national broadcasting service must prevail."
I wish to apologize for not having written out the amendment itself. There may be many places in the country in which the C.B.C. wants to establish its own

stations and there is already a private station in operation, but it can only do that when the government makes the necessary money available to it. It seems to me that the members of the regulatory authority are going to use some sense in coming to their decisions.
We have the current examples already mentioned of Saskatoon, Sudbury, Victoria,
B.	C. and St. John's, Newfoundland, where the
C.	B.C. would like to establish stations, but it is not going to be able to do so because the government will not make the necessary funds available. The problem is not as real or as big as some hon. members think it is.

Does the hon. member not feel that the public interest should be the deciding factor and not the national broadcasting service? Which should be the deciding, overwhelming and paramount factor, the public interest or the objectives of the national broadcasting service?

I am sure the hon. member will not consider this a satisfactory reply but I wish to point out that what we are talking about is an extension of the national broadcasting service. These places will get that national service either through a publicly owned station or through a privately owned station which becomes affiliated with the C.B.C.

The hon. member for Burna-by-Richmond has stated the case quite well but there is one qualification. In my presence not more than 48 hours ago a key figure in the C.B.C., speaking at a public meeting, said it was an objective of the C.B.C., where alternative service was a consideration, to establish its own station. The case in point was Kingston. The policy of the C.B.C. as of this moment, and presumably it has not yet been changed by the new executive, is to apply for a licence for a second station wherever a privately owned station exists and where there is a demand for alternative service. There has been no clarification whether the
Canadian Policy on Broadcasting C.B.C. interpretation of this as an objective is in agreement with the government's position regarding the objectives of the C.B.C.
At present there are requests for a second service in 10 or 12 centres, and until the new regulatory agency knows whether the C.B.C. is going to put its own facilities in those centres these communities will be confined to a single service. Here is a case where I suggest the objectives of the national service, as outlined in this clause, would almost require the regulatory agency to say that these communities must wait on the availability of C.B.C. funds in order to get a second service through a C.B.C. station.

Mr. Chairman, I can agree with much of what the hon. member has said. It is true that the C.B.C. wants to establish its own stations in a number of places. But what is required is long-range capital policy planning. I think it will be the duty of the government to make known to the C.B.C. very soon what capital funds will be made available to it during the next few years. If it is not going to have capital funds made available to it to build stations in ten different places but just enough for three or four places, this should be made known to the C.B.C. and then the regulatory authority could be guided by that information. If the C.B.C. cannot get the funds to establish a station in Kingston for the next ten years, then the regulatory authority will be guided by that fact. If the authority knew there would be only a two year delay they might postpone a private application. What is needed is long-range capital planning, with the details made known to the C.B.C. and to the regulatory authority.

Canadian Policy on Broadcasting expect private stations to do the kind of programming which we expect and have been able to get from the public broadcasting system.
That being the case I think it is our responsibility and the responsibility of the regulatory agency, not to take steps which will freeze out the C.B.C. in these centres which have been mentioned. To take Kingston, the example mentioned by the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo, if the C.B.C. is frozen out the people there will not have an opportunity in the foreseeable future to get the kind of programming which only the C.B.C. has done and is doing. speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this is my first attempt to take part in this debate. It is not my intention to delay unduly the passage of this bill. However, I find that this subclause as it stood originally and as it stands now as amended is absolutely incompatible with all the beliefs I, as a citizen of this country, hold.
Without presenting a political philosophy of any kind I should like to point out some of the logic which I believe hon. members should apply to this subclause before we give final consideration to it. The original subclause in the bill would make the national broadcasting service paramount in this country. From reading the bill one can only come to the conclusion that if there should be any difference between the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and any of the private stations the solution to the problem would, ipso facto, be in favour of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. The exact wording of subclause (h) of clause 2 is as follows:
-where any conflict arises between the objectives of the national broadcasting service and interests of the private element of the Canadian broadcasting system, the objectives of the national broadcasting service must prevail;
In other words, it matters not one iota what the reasons might be for the objectives of the private broadcasters if the objectives of the national broadcasting service which are being put forward are in the least contrary to the action being pursued by the private broadcasters. In this case the objectives of the national broadcasting service must prevail.
The next question we must ask ourselves is, who shall decide what are the objectives of the commission. A little farther on in the bill we find, under the heading "Powers of the Council", clause 16. Clause 16 reads as follows:
(1) In furtherance of Its objects, the Council, on the recommendation of the Executive Committee, may
(a) prescribe classes of broadcasting licences;-
Tebruary 1, 1968	COMMONS
I do not find that reprehensible. However, I *do find paragraph (b) reprehensible. It reads as follows:
(b) make regulations applicable to all persons holding broadcasting licences, or to all persons holding broadcasting licences of one or more classes,
(i)	respecting standards of programs,
(ii)	respecting scheduling policy in relation to any category or categories of programs,
(iii)	respecting the character of advertising and the amount of time that may be devoted to advertising,
(iv)	respecting the proportion of time that may be devoted to the broadcasting of programs, advertisements or announcements of a partisan political character and the assignment of such time on an equitable basis to political parties and candidates,
(v)	respecting the use of dramatization in programs, advertisements or announcements of a partisan political character,
Paragraph (b) lists in all nine fields in which the executive committee of the council can establish its own objectives and make regulations. In other words, the members of the council are empowered to establish and enforce their own objectives. Once again it is a case of setting up a body somewhat like a bureaucratic group of civil servants which can make its own laws, enforce those laws and make a final judgment from which there is no appeal.
I suggest to hon. members that the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Ed-monton-Strathcona should not be dismissed without serious consideration. As a matter of fact, while I was in the house yesterday the hon. member for Winnipeg South proposed an amendment which put the case very clearly. The effect of his amendment would have been to make the public interest paramount in respect of any consideration given to quarrels between the private and public sectors of broadcasting. It seemed to me that the amendment proposed by the hon. member suited the purpose admirably because we are here not to protect the C.B.C. but rather to protect the public interest.
My friends to the left, geographically and politically, say it is the same thing. It is far from being the same thing. One does not protect the rights of individuals or private enterprise by assigning the rights to some government bureaucracy. This House of Commons is the root of government. We assign some of our authority to ministers but ministers are answerable to this house. From past experience we know that the authority which has been vested in organizations, committees
DEBATES	6253
Canadian Policy on Broadcasting and commissions such as the Board of Broadcast Governors or the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation is not defended before the bar of the House of Commons. There have been many occasions since I have been a member of this house when questions, particularly concerning the character of programs, have been raised in respect of the C.B.C., at which time the minister has stated that answers to the questions cannot be given in the House of Commons because the C.B.C. is not responsible to her.
I say that the subclause as placed in the bill originally and as now amended gives very great authority to the commission which will be governing broadcasting in this country henceforth. I would agree to this amendment or to the original subclause if we had any indication of agreement from the broadcasting industry of this country that that industry should be subjected to this type of regulation. Without having inquired of the private broadcasters, I feel quite sure that no private broadcaster in this country would be agreeable to or suggest such a provision as subclause (h). I dare say that the Canadian Association of Broadcasters finds this subclause very reprehensible, because it will hold back the private sector of broadcasting in this country in order to make way for a slowly moving and lethargic publicly owned broadcasting system.
I do not believe it is good enough for some members of this house to rise and say that the private broadcasters of this country have not done a good job. I think the private broadcasters have been pushing the C.B.C. into more and better programming. The private broadcasters have been leading the way in broadcasting in this country and deserve better treatment than we are offering them under subclause (h) of clause 2.

I say to the minister that if she can rise in her place and say that the Canadian Association of Broadcasters is in complete agreement with subclause (h) and thinks it will not inhibit their growth, ingenuity and adventurous spirit, I will take a different attitude to it. I refer to those hon. members who realize that the passage of this subclause will put television and radio in this country under a cloud and will mean that

Canadian Policy on Broadcasting producers in the private sector will be apprehensive of any type of exploration in programming for fear that it may offend a member of the broadcasting commission.
Therefore I would like the minister to give me the assurance at this time that the Canadian Association of Broadcasters, whose members represent the private broadcasting sector of the country, are not opposed to this subclause. Otherwise I would urge hon. members to amend the subclause so that it will read along the lines put forward yesterday by the hon. member for Winnipeg South, to the effect that decisions will be made after giving consideration, and only consideration, to the public interest. Mr. Chairman, I did not expect to have to stand again-
Who told you to?
-to comment upon this subclause.

If the hon. lady would stand and say what I think she should say it would be quite unnecessary for me to rise again to speak on the bill. It is the hon. lady who opened the lid of Pandora's box. It is she who knows better than anybody, I hope, where the C.B.C. has got off the track. I have assured the hon. lady on more than one occasion, and I repeat it now, that if she is going to look after the best interests of the people of Canada I will pack up and sit down. speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: Or of being a tool.

Crown corporations are a danger in that, in my opinion, they are an abdication of free enterprise. They are enabled, through the power of government, to do some things which some people in government think are not capable of being performed by private enterprise.
I shall repeat as often as I can, that I believe private enterprise can perform any service for the people of Canada better than ponderous crown corporations. Some crown

corporations are slow in their empire building, but the C.B.C. is not. The C.B.C. has an over-burgeoning budget which has reached, I believe, some $170 million a year. I do not think their budget will go down. Yet we appear to be receiving less and less real service in the public interest.
What can be done about this situation? We certainly will not improve it by increasing the powers of this crown corporation to the point where they can blot out all competition from private interests. When I hear members of the house applauding this bill and the particular subclause under discussion, I know we are getting to the heart of the matter and they are pleasing those people who want to blot out all competition from private enterprise.
I admit there may be times when a crown corporation does give us service. We vote them the money to do this. But I venture to say that never, but never, does a crown corporation give us better service, dollar for dollar, than private enterprise. If you put unlimited funds at the disposal of a crown corporation, how can private enterprise hope to compete?
Private enterprise has proved time and time again that in the broadcasting field it can put programs on the air for a fraction of the money that is taken out of the taxpayers' pockets for the C.B.C Surely this alone is a good reason why this subclause should not be passed. If it does pass, there will be no competition whatsoever as long as the C.B.C. wants it that way. Surely all we are doing here, unless we are to have a co-operative system in Canada, is getting out guide lines. The guide lines in respect of the C.B.C have been ignored continually during the last three or four years. The objectives as outlined in subclause (g) have always been those laid down by parliament as guide lines for the C.B.C. But there is no question at all that today the people of Canada are convinced that these guide lines have not been followed.
The reason given for the C.B.C. not following these guide lines is that there must be freedom of the air. How can this subclause give freedom of the air when it cuts out all possible competition to the C.B.C.? I could not agree more with my colleague the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona when he says he cannot vote for anything which purports to put itself above the public interest. I am not satisfied so far that the definition of public interest is what I and, I sincerely believe, the people of Canada think is the public interest.
February 1, 1968

Let me refer to the objectives as set out in subclause (g). I do not say this in ignorance of the real issues but the question is, who is going to carry out these objectives, if they are going to be carried out at all? My argument is well founded if put forward only on monetary grounds. I think I have covered that question. It is more economical for private enterprise to provide good programming.
However, we know that private enterprise has, naturally, a selfish interest. It is looking for profit. In spite of the fact that private enterprise can provide programs more cheaply and, I think, more effectively in a great many cases, it naturally wants to avoid the non-profitable areas of broadcasting. It is not particularly interested in education for education's sake. Private enterprise cannot afford to provide high-powered stations to cover the hinterland, the deep north, the outlying districts. Naturally, true free enterprise is concerned with making a profit and wants to reach the most people for the least amount of money.
A progressive government wants to cover non-profitable operations, particularly if it will mean national unity, education, Canadian identity and the bringing of culture to our people. As taxpayers we have been willing up to now to pay a very large subsidy to this crown corporation which has by and large covered these areas. I like to think that this is a stopgap measure and eventually the population of Canada will expand to the point where every section of our country can afford free enterprise coverage, which is cheaper and can better depict public opinion.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
Even if the C.B.C. were to carry out the objectives outlined in subclause (g), it would still be a government fed organization. Both the hon. lady and the C.B.C. say they do not want to be told what programs to put on. I for one do not want to have to tell them in detail what programs to put on, but I am quite certain that unless the C.B.C. has competition and unless it has guidance from above, it will continue to provide the type of program we have had until now and which is not acceptable to us. Therefore we are forced to try to improve the bill which alone can delegate the powers and lay down the guide lines for this vast corporation.
The C.B.C. is not the only crown corporation which has got out of hand. The first trip I made as a member representing my great constituency was to Montreal for an interview
Canadian Policy on Broadcasting with the head of the Canadian National Railways. Before I could even introduce myself or put forward the proposition which I went down there to present to the C.N.R. I was told, "Go home to Alberta, mind your own business and leave our railroad alone". What did they mean by "our railroad"? One might have thought they meant the railroad of the public of Canada. However, that is not what they meant at all. They meant that the C.N.R. was a power unto itself and that even members of parliament should not be allowed to question its officers on whether or not they could give a better service to the areas represented by members. This is just not good enough. At that time I stated to the C.N.R. that I was not a baby and that I happened to represent 70,000 people who wanted an improvement in the service. But I was told it was none of my business. It is my business to do something about what I think is wrong, and this also applies to the C.B.C.
I can tell from the smiles on the faces of hon. members opposite that they think Mr. Donald Gordon was right and I was wrong and that I am still wrong. I do not think there is any institution in Canada above parliament, and whenever we delegate powers to ministers, to the government generally or to officials of the C.B.C., all we are doing is saying that we are seized with the responsibility of looking after the public interests of Canada. I am heartened that there are a great many members of the house who will at least try to ensure that the public interest is safeguarded. I venture to suggest that the people of Canada look to us to ensure that this is done. I for one am not willing to abdicate the regulatory power which we have and to say that any goup of people, no matter how strong and how well informed they may be, can stand above parliament and say that their ideas of what the public interests are should be paramount.
It is often difficult for us to agree on what exactly the public interest is at any one time. As my friends to the left would say, one must sometimes go on and on trying until the necessary action is taken. The divorce bill is a good example. The members of that party were commended in many quarters in Canada for the way in which they worked almost ad nauseam until some result was achieved and finally action was taken. Our divorce laws are being very carefully considered.

Order, please. I have listened to the hon. member speaking about railroads and now about
6256	COMMONS
Canadian Policy on Broadcasting divorce and I wonder whether it might not be better if he would confine his remarks to the subclause under discussion, namely subclause (h).
speakername: @Deputy Chair(man)? of Committees of the Whole

speechtext:
Subclause (h) refers to one thing only, the public interest, how it can best be served and how the parliament of Canada should delegate its authority, to whom and why. I do not think I have wandered away from this broad reference because "public interest" is a very broad subject. Every section of Canada's public life is affected by this subclause and any possible amendments thereto. It affects the very roots of democracy itself. I believe I should not abdicate my responsibilities in this respect because we are dealing here with a matter which has a bearing on democracy or, if you like, bureaucracy, and there are people who believe that only through complete bureaucracy can there be freedom. I say that when bureaucracy predominates and becomes paramount there is no freedom.
Such a state of affairs may arise when there is an abuse of power on the part of crown corporations such as, for instance, the C.N.R. I do not think any member in the house who takes his responsibilities seriously would agree that a member of a crown corporation should say to me when I go to see him about an improvement for the welfare of my people that I should go home and mind my own business, even before I have stated my case. The case I intended to put to the C.N.R. involved the extension of two railroad lines, one of which was built and the other was not. One of them was the Pine Point railroad. If I had an interest in a private broadcasting station and sought to compete with the C.B.C. I would not want to receive the same answer I received from the C.N.R., that the matter is in hand, that they are handling it adequately, that they know all the answers and will give all the service necessary regardless of the cost to the taxpayer and regardless of whether or not the objectives outlined in subclause (g) are in fact being carried out.
Those who believe in free enterprise in Canada have a right to speak out. It is passing strange that if the people of Canada do not think so they should vote the way they do. The people of Canada not only want the free enterprise system to prevail but they are getting tired of our sitting here in the House of Commons and not doing something about improving the opportunity of people under free enterprise to earn a living.
[The Assistant Deputy Chairman.]
DEBATES	February 1, 1966
The complaint we hear more often than any other concerns how much, if anything, is being done in Ottawa to preserve the free enterprise system. Do we still believe in an honest profit for honest work or must we all become children of the state? I am tired of the fatherly approach. I, for one, am tired of being looked after from birth to eternity. Perhaps the only vestige of individual freedom left is the freedom to stand here and waste the time of some people. I assure you I am not wasting the time of the people who sent me here. If I want to keep coming down here, my only fear is that I may lose my nerve and not continue to fight for free enterprise, for the right of a man to earn a living and the right to compete with crown corporations no matter how much sanctity those corporations think they have.
[DOT] (5:00 p.m.)
There is no such thing as a crown corporation that is above parliament. We cannot abdicate the public interest and we do not intend to do so. If you have an ear to the ground, as I have, and if you listen to what the little people of Canada are saying you will find they want the government to withdraw from the business fields it occupies in Canada. These people want the right to compete, to put their time and energy behind their own self-interest and be good, free Canadian citizens.
There are a great many people in this country who still believe that the free enterprise system is the most effective, the most fair economically, the most challenging and the most satisfying which has ever been developed on this tired old planet of ours. I look at those areas of the world which do not have our system and I find there is not a citizen in Canada who would be willing to go there. The only reason it is worth while to stay here is that we intend to preserve this system as long as we have the power to do so. I still believe the people of Canada are going to insist that we have the courage to stand here and criticize each and every attempt to put the interests of any group above the interests of the people of Canada. It is not beyond our capability to spell out in each and every statute which we put on the books a provision that this gang over here or that gang over there shall not be preferred. As I take my seat I assure you that when legislation is proposed which will put the public interest above all other interests I will be the first to support it.
February 1, 1968

Mr. Chairman, I am glad to see that the Leader of the Opposition is in the chamber because I think he can be of some assistance to us in this debate. It seems quite evident that some members of his party are determined to filibuster this clause.
Oh, oh.
I do not know what the views of the official opposition are in connection with broadcasting matters.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, please. The hon. member for Winnipeg South on a point of order.

I think the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond would like to reconsider his remark about filibustering. There has been no filibuster in this committee by anyone, particularly anyone on this side of the chamber. We have had a deep and urgent interest in this legislation. I feel that the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond would like to reconsider his remark.
No, Mr. Chairman, I would not like to reconsider it. I said what I thought was a correct interpretation of the situation now.

I rise on the point of order, Mr. Chairman. I looked at the citation in Beau-chesne a couple of days ago and found that a member of this house cannot impute motives to another hon. member. If the hon. member does not have enough courtesy to withdraw his remark, then I ask the chairman to make a ruling on the matter.
I did not impute any motives to the hon. member for York-Humber. If I had to do so-
I said the reference was to any member, not to me.
The hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond did impute motives to certain members of the party of the Leader of the Opposition. He so identified the people to whom he referred.
If the hon. member for Winnipeg South had listened carefully he would have noticed that I qualified my remarks and did not include the Leader of the Opposition.
Withdraw.

I shall now continue with what I was going to say. I should like to know
Canadian Policy on Broadcasting what the views of the Leader of the Opposition are on broadcasting matters and what is the broadcasting policy of his party. I suspect his views are more in line with the views of the hon. member for Royal and the hon. member for Halifax, to whom we have listened this afternoon, in connection with this clause. If we could hear his views perhaps we could make some progress on this matter.
Some members have spoken this afternoon as if private broadcasting in Canada were in peril because of subclause (h), but it certainly is not. There are more private television and radio stations in Canada at the moment than there are C.B.C. stations, and there will be more in the future. Some of them are doing very well. There is no reason why private stations will not do well in the future. There is nothing in this bill which will prevent private broadcasters from establishing new stations and making money.
What the bill provides is certain objectives of broadcasting policy, and those objectives are given to the national broadcasting service to carry out. The national broadcasting service may consist of publicly owned stations or of privately owned stations affiliated with the C.B.C. They are charged with this specific responsibility. When I tried to move an amendment to impose the objective of national unity upon all broadcasters in Canada I was told that this was a special job for the public element. We are giving them this special job, so it seems to me they should have a paramount position. There is nothing in the bill which will inhibit private broadcasting. We are being subjected to delaying tactics, so I think it would help if we could hear from a spokesman for the official opposition as to what their broadcasting policy is.

Mr. Chairman, we are witnessing another attempt to get back to where we were something like a day and a half ago in the discussion of clause 2(h). I am not at all happy with the amendment that is before us. It suggests that all other things being equal the scales should be tipped toward the public corporation. Surely the task of any board adjudicating a conflict that might arise between the objectives of the national broadcasting service and the interests of the private element would be to determine which side had the better case. If they arrive at a point where, all other factors being in balance, they are unable to make a decision, then their clear duty would be to resign or at least to pass on the dispute to the next level or reconstitute the board so new personnel
6258	COMMONS
Canadian Policy on Broadcasting could examine the question to ascertain which side had the better case. We do not need or want in this legislation a guide line that would inevitably tip the scales in one direction. It would not take many precedents to establish a rule embedded more firmly than the wording of the amendment before us might suggest.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
It has already been suggested by one provincial figure that passage of this bill should be postponed till the conclusion of the constitutional conference. In view of the Canadian charter of human rights to be presented to the conference, this might be a good idea. For example, in this booklet that has been distributed to hon. members there is a reference to the United States declaration of independence and we read that all men are created equal and endowed with inalienable rights, such as life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness. We also read that to secure these rights governments are instituted among men deriving their just powers from the consent of the governed, and whenever any form of government becomes destructive of these ends we are not to tip the scales in its favour but it is the right of the people to alter or abolish it and to institute a new government.
These are very clear and ringing words in support of the argument that has been carried on for the past two days that the public interest, the government interest or the interest of crown corporations need not be identical. This is a point that seems to require a tremendous amount of reiteration.
Again in the booklet provided to hon. members, Mr. Chairman, we read the following:
In both the United States and France, there was embodied the idea that men shall not be deprived of liberty or property except in accordance with the law. This is a manifestation of the belief that men should be ruled by laws, not men; that a government has no more power than the people have agreed to delegate to it.
I hope this parliament will not be willing to delegate to the government more than its equal share of power in any dispute that may arise between the objectives of the national broadcasting service and private interests. There will be occasions when the private interest is not that of one individual who would come into dispute with the objectives of the national broadcasting service at some point in the future.
The charter of human rights from which I have quoted suggests that Canada needs a constitutional bill of rights. I am not prepared
IMr. Johnston.]
DEBATES	February 1, 1968
at the moment to argue that we need that constitutional guarantee as long as we have a parliament that is alert and courts that use their wisdom to decide cases between parties, not on the basis of some prearranged criterion that the government of the day might wish them to use.
I should like to read one further paragraph from this charter. At page 11 there is this statement:
A constitutional bill of rights in Canada would guarantee the fundamental freedoms of the individual from interference, whether federal or provincial.
That is a brave declaration, Mr. Chairman, in light of the fact that we seem to be prepared to write into this broadcasting bill a certain amount of interference with the individual and to say that where all things are considered equal the scale is to be tipped in favour of the crown corporation, whose interest is to be paramount. Perhaps it would be well from the point of view of the government to consider the broadcasting bill in relation to the Canadian charter of human rights, and it might also be a good idea to wait until the conference has concluded before proceeding further with this bill.

Mr. Chairman, like the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond, I have some difficulty in detecting just what is the position of the official opposition on this question, and I think it is important that this be clarified. One of the benefits of our parliamentary system is that a party in this house can take a position that the people of Canada can later judge when they are given the opportunity to choose a government. I suggest that we in this house are not giving the people of Canada that opportunity until we determine what is the official opposition's position on this very basic paragraph in the bill.
The hon. member for Okanagan-Revelstoke stated quite clearly what I presumed to be the position of his party. The hon. member for Athabasca stated quite clearly what may be the position of his party, though I am not sure. It seemed to differ substantially from the position taken in the past, both in the house and in committee, by the hon. member for Royal, who I understood to be the broadcasting expert and critic for the official opposition. It also seemed to differ substantially from the position taken by the member I understood to be the deputy broadcasting critic for the official opposition, the hon. member for Halifax.
February 1, 1968

Yesterday we saw the spectacle of the hon. member for Halifax being abandoned, except for the companionship of the house leader of the official opposition, in his introduction of an amendment which those of us on this side of the house-certainly the minister-took in good faith as an amendment put forward on behalf of his party. I believe the minister went to some trouble to check with the broadcasting critic of the N.D.P. in order to see whether the amendment was acceptable to that party, though perhaps not with the hon. member for Okanagan-Revelstoke because the position of his party has been very clearly stated. It is not a position with which I agree but I believe he has stated it clearly. I believe that we and the people of Canada have the right to know clearly what is the position of the official opposition on this point, one that is so central to the future of broadcasting in Canada.
It has been suggested that this subclause, either as originally worded or as amended on the initiative of the hon. member for Halifax, the deputy broadcasting critic of the official opposition, undermines democracy. Is that the position taken by the Progressive Conservative party? It seems to me that the position taken by the government is clear: it is that put forward by the minister responsible. Every member of this party on this side of the house does not completely agree with that position, but we all know what is the position of the government. Do we know what is the position of the official opposition? I am afraid I have not been able to ascertain it.
Does the official opposition agree or not with the original exposition of the place of public broadcasting given by Right Hon. R.
B.	Bennett some years ago and quoted so often during the debate, and which occupies such an important place in the report of the committee of which I have the honour to be chairman? I suggest there is nothing original in the wording of the subclause put forward by the minister. Subclause (h) is new to the Broadcasting Act, or will be if it is passed, but it is surely not new to our consideration of broadcasting in Canada.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
When that great senior statesman of Canadian broadcasting, Mr. E. Austin Weir, made a statement to our committee during our consideration of the white paper on broadcasting, he said that a score of parliamentary committees from 1932 to 1958 and two royal commissions had declared the
C.	B.C. to be the core and dominant feature of
Canadian Policy on Broadcasting the Canadian broadcasting system. He said the white paper prepared by the government did not state that predominance and he recommended, as did other witnesses, that it be stated and that our new act should make a legislative declaration of the predominance of the public sector of broadcasting.
This desire was recognized by the committee, as demonstrated by the hon. lady, in a number of places in the report which was tabled in the house on March 21, 1967. I shall refer to a few passages to indicate what this all-party committee had to say about this matter. On page 6 of the report, under our comments on section 3 of the white paper, are found these words:
The committee concurs with the general principles stated in the white paper. We urge, however, a clear legislative declaration of the pre-eminence of the public sector.
On page 7, at the beginning of paragraph 4 of our comments, are found the following words:
The C.B.C., as the prime instrument of public policy in broadcasting and one of the world's largest broadcasting organizations, needs a strong board of directors.
You will note the words "prime instrument of public policy in broadcasting".
On page 8 of our report, still commenting on paragraph 4 of the white paper, we said:
In assessing the C.B.C., the B.B.G. should take into account the financial resources available to the corporation, its mandate and its vital importance as the prime instrument of national policy in broadcasting.
Though this matter has been mentioned a number of times in the house it must be mentioned again, and I refer to the last paragraph of the report which is in italics to emphasize the importance each member of the committee attached to the statement I am about to read:
We express our conviction that the primacy of the public sector should be the paramount and continuing objective of the new legislation; that we must make more effective, and not undermine, the main instrument by which "national consciousness may be fostered and sustained and national unity still further strengthened."
The last words "national consciousness may be fostered and sustained and national unity still further strengthened" are a direct quotation of the words of Right Hon. R. B. Bennett, spoken when he introduced the legislation founding the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation 35-odd years ago. That position has been adopted in many reports, but now I wish to refer briefly to the latest basis
8260	COMMONS
Canadian Policy on Broadcasting for public policy in this field. The report of the committee on broadcasting, 1965, better known as the second Fowler report, says on page 12:
We believe that private broadcasters can, and should, achieve a greater degree of common purpose, and should participate in the national objectives of the Canadian broadcasting system to which they belong, as well as continuing to render local services to their individual communities. But the private sector is unlikely to achieve the cohesion and unity that the public sector should have and, despite their near equality in total income, this necessarily means that the public agency -the C.B.C.-has the primary responsibility and must be paramount in creating and maintaining a broadcasting system that is distinctively Canadian.
While the private broadcasters are a part of the system, and while their rights and interests should have all legitimate protection, in cases of fundamental conflict between the public and private sectors the interests of the C.B.C. must prevail.
I shall leave that quotation for a moment to say that the drafters of this legislation recognized that perhaps that statement is too strong. They have carefully distinguished between the objectives of the public sector and the interests of the private sector and they have not placed the interests of the C.B.C. above the interests of the private sector. I continue quoting:
The simple fact-the crucial fact-which must be clearly understood is that the C.B.C. is the essential-
That last word is in italics:
-element of the Canadian broadcasting system and the most important single instrument available for the development and maintenance of the unity of Canada.
Also, on page 123 of this same report appear these statements:
The C.B.C. is the chosen instrument for public broadcasting in Canada. It is only a part of the Canadian broadcasting system; the private broadcasters also receive rights to use public assets and, in accepting those rights assume responsibilities to contribute to the national purpose of the system. However, the C.B.C. has the primary responsibility for providing excellent broadcasting services to the Canadian people.
Lower down on that page appears this statement:
Having been given the primary responsibility, the interests of the C.B.C. are paramount within the Canadian broadcasting system, but if it is to perform its function adequately and acceptably, it must be told what it is expected to do. It must have a clear mandate from parliament.
I interpose to say that that is one of the objects of clause 2 and particularly of subclause (g) which has already been passed, I believe. Returning to the report, I quote from page 125:
It should be clearly stated:-

DEBATES	February 1, 1968
I skip a paragraph and continue quoting:
-that within the national system, the C.B.C., as the chosen instrument of parliament, has the prime responsibility to provide broadcasting services to the Canadian people as a whole, and that the interests of the C.B.C. are therefore paramount.
In making its recommendations to the house the standing committee reflected the basic statements and principles which appear in the second Fowler report and in other similar reports which have been made through the years. I am delighted, as I am sure the majority of our committee members are, that the minister and the government recognized the necessity to make the clear legislative declaration that the objects of the public sector should be paramount. It is not only the majority of Liberal members of that committee, not only the majority of the official opposition on that committee-its chief critic was a member of the steering committee and helped to draft our report- not only the majority of N.D.P. members of that committee and not only those who drafted this legislation who have supported the concept and sentiment about which I have spoken and read. There was editorial comment following the release of our report, and I want to refer to two editorials which state the case clearly. One of these articles appeared in the Ottawa Citizen of March 22, 1967, and I quote from it in reference to the report of our committee:
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
It strongly affirms the pre-eminent role which the publicly-owned Canadian Broadcasting Corporation should play in a national system.
Later the article says:
It has taken the best of Fowler and of the white paper, but has sharpened the main points of both and has kept in view the national purposes and special value of a public broadcasting organization.
Some members of the opposition might suggest that the Ottawa Citizen is more favourably disposed toward the government than are certain other newspapers. To please them I should like to quote from the Ottawa Journal of the same date in which these words appear in an editorial on the subject of our report:
The basic importance of the committee's work is to reaffirm the role of the C.B.C. in Canadian broadcasting. Members of parliament from all sides of the Commons urge "a clear, legislative declaration of the pre-eminence of the public sector"- the C.B.C.
It is clear what all the bodies which have investigated broadcasting in this country over the years have recommended. It is clear what
February 1, 1968

the standing committee on broadcasting wanted. The government has made its position clear by adopting the recommendations of the standing committee. The hon. member for Okanagan-Revelstoke has made the position of his party clear and the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond has made the position of the New Democratic party clear. I wonder whether we could ask that the position of the official opposition be made clear at this point. Let members opposite tell us whether they are opposed to the principles I have just outlined. If, indeed, they are opposed to those principles, let us hear their position clearly stated. Let them, if necessary, put forward a further amendment to express their attitude. Then let the committee vote on it and make progress with this bill. It is incumbent on the party opposite and in particular, as the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond stated, it is incumbent on the leader of that party to tell us what he thinks about this broadcasting legislation.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I have a few brief remarks to make on the bill before us, particularly with regard to the amendment suggested by the hon. member for Calgary. It has been the custom for most speakers to deal briefly with the general subject of radio and television in relation to this subclause of the bill. Many speeches have been made in the course of the last few weeks on the subject matter of this important bill. It is only since I have been paying particular attention to the bill in the last few days that I have become aware of the fact that there is such dissension and disruption in the ranks of the official opposition relating to their whole philosophy of their approach to broadcasting. I respect the hon. member for Calgary, who has spoken on a number of occasions and who spent a long time in the standing committee-
On a point of order, is the hon. member referring to the hon. member for Calgary South or does he have the hon. member for Winnipeg South in mind?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext:
Both hon. gentlemen. The point I am making is that we have advanced a long way during our consideration of this bill, the foundation for which is the acceptance among all parties, with the exception perhaps of the Social Credit party, of a political philosophy generally favourable toward the C.B.C. and the advance of public funds annually in its support. This does not mean that the C.B.C is above criticism. Indeed, there is no other public body which has been
Canadian Policy on Broadcasting subject to as much criticism and investigation. But at least we believed that the Conservative party, along with the Liberal party and the New Democratic party, approved the concept of the public radio and television organization which we call the C.B.C. It is only as a result of the dissension and disunity which is so evident from the speeches of hon. members of the official opposition that we begin to realize there is an internal struggle going on within the party opposite as to whether it does or does not endorse the principle upon which the C.B.C. was established.
I recognize and understand the views of those who have indicated in the last few days that they are against public broadcasting or television. The former leader of the opposition never missed an opportunity in the House of Commons, even when castigating the C.B.C., to re-endorse the principle that a country as close to the United States as we are needed some organization such as the C.B.C. to represent what little Canadian identity we have left in this nation.
The C.B.C. is among the few media of communication that we control in this country through which we can emphasize the fact that we are a country and a nation. It is for this reason, because the C.B.C. has such a responsible role to play in the growth of this country, that we have adopted subclause (g) and outlined the four broad objectives of the corporation. In these circumstances I think it is about time the Leader of the Opposition let us know where he stands. Does he support the spokesmen for private enterprise over there or does he support those who believe in the C.B.C.?
Would the hon. member permit a question? Would he be more explicit and tell the committee on what occasion anybody in this party has spoken against the idea of a publicly-owned broadcasting system?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext:
Yes. Only the other night the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings openly stated that he was contemplating bringing in an amendment whose effect would be to destroy the whole concept of a publicly-owned system. One would only have to read some of the speeches made today to realize that all too many members of the official opposition are against the C.B.C. and that when the chips are down they stand for private interests, the profit-making organizations.
Here, as I say, is a medium of communication which was designed to protect the
6262	COMMONS
Canadian Policy on Broadcasting Canadian identity. And what do we hear from members of the official opposition? They object to the word "filibuster". If the word "filibuster" is too strong for their sensitive feelings, let us examine the history of the bill before us. Is it something brought up by the minister last week, something which is being rammed through the House of Commons? If it were a filibuster would be legitimate or at least understandable. But what are the facts? The facts show that the C.B.C. has been subject-
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)

Mr. Chairman, on a point of order.
In wonder if the member for Verdun (Mr. Mackasey) is dealing with the amendment now under consideration or whether he is doing a history of the opposition party. The Chair has often called us to order when we strayed from the question or from the amendment under consideration.
I realize the hon. member has strayed quite far from the subject and I wonder if he should not stick to the paragraph (h) of clause 2 so that we may make some progress? Why does the member wish to prolong consideration of this bill?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext:
On the point of order, Mr. Chairman, it is obvious that the objection to clause 2(h) is an objection to the principle that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation should exist, is existing, and should have priority over private interests in this country. This is all the objection really is. One group is supporting private interests and the other group, including myself at the moment, is supporting and defending the principle that surely this country should have some medium controlled by parliament, belonging to the Canadian people, and dedicated to the concept that we are a nation and that Americans do not and should not control all our fields of communications. This concept is reflected in subclause (h).
We have had intensive investigations of the C.B.C. and its operations. Just a few months ago hon. gentlemen who are now castigating the C.B.C. took advantage of a statement made by the minister, in which she suggested there was rotten management in the C.B.C., to stand up and protect the C.B.C. and castigate the minister. If we had time to compare their statements then with their statements now it would make funny reading. However,

DEBATES	February 1, 1968
as a result of certain studies and investigations we came up with a white paper which formed the basis of this bill.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I would ask the hon. member to confine his remarks as closely as possible to clause 2(h).

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext:
I entirely agree with your suggestion, Mr. Chairman, and as usual bow to your ruling. As amended clause 2(h) now reads:
(h) where any conflict arises between the objectives of the national broadcasting service and the interests of the private element of the Canadian broadcasting system, it shall be resolved in the public interest but paramount consideration shall be given to the objectives of the national broadcasting service.
I think this was a fine amendment of the subclause. I presume it was drawn up by the hon. member for Halifax. I am not certain of that, but it sounds very much like his work because it does not depart from the principle that the C.B.C. is our organization, for better or worse, as opposed to that of private interests, and it also recognizes the rights of those private interests to a fair hearing in areas of conflict.
But that amendment has not satisfied all the members of the Conservative party, despite the fact that it was brought forward by a member as senior, as respected and as intelligent as the hon. member for Halifax. This can only lead to the conclusion that there is a definite difference of opinion in that party. This is a fair assumption because if it did meet the full approval of the Conservative party and reflected their philosophy and policy vis-a-vis the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, this clause would have been passed long ago and the committee would have moved on to another clause.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Is the house ready for the question?
Mr. Colin Cameron (Nanaimo-Cowichan-
The Islands): Mr. Speaker, as I am sure most hon. members have become aware, I and some of my colleagues are quite concerned about the steady flow into this chamber of bills to incorporate more and more life insurance companies. I may say that our concern is shared by the Inspector General of Insurance, who at a committee hearing some months ago said that he and his departmental officials were quite concerned about the continual incorporation of more and more life insurance companies and were asking themselves

whether this was really necessary for the good of the Canadian economy. He also pointed out, quite rightly, at that time that neither he nor his officials were in a position to say: This is enough; we cut if off here. As the Inspector General of Insurance quite correctly pointed out to the committee, if we allow one Canadian citizen to hold a policy in a life insurance company every Canadian citizen must have this right.
At that particular committee meeting I suggested it was time the government and parliament began to look into the whole question of the savings of the Canadian people and the manner in which they were to be treated, because the basis of all economic development and progress in an economy is the savings of the economy in the form of personal savings of citizens and surpluses from business operations. It is of vital importance that we should have some control and direction of these savings for the development of the Canadian economy and Canadian society.
The continual proliferation of private life insurance companies is splintering the pool of savings. As far as I can see the only effect is to contribute to the chaos that has obtained for quite a long time now in our financial institutions, a chaos that occasionally results in the collapse of businesses of various sorts, a chaos that eventually causes financial troubles that create problems for the government and limit the development of our society and economy. We have been urging again and again in the house that the parliament and government of Canada should take a very long, hard look at this business of bringing in new bills to incorporate still more life insurance companies.
I should like to see the whole matter referred to a parliamentary committee or perhaps even to a commission of inquiry to investigate the net results of permitting the savings of the Canadian people to fall into the hands of private groups which have complete control over the manner in which those savings shall be invested, whether in the Canadian economy or some other economy. Far too much of the savings of the Canadian people collected by life insurance companies and mutual funds is invested in another economy. At the same time, of course, we hear continual pleas by government spokesmen that Canada requires a continual inflow of capital from abroad if we are to continue to exist, let alone expand.
February 1, 1968

I have for a long time, sir, been protesting that this is looking at only one part of the picture. I have complained that the government of Canada, this and previous governments, has been in the habit of pleading with our United States friends to lend us their money while at the same time allowing Canadian capital to flow out of the economy. I suggest that if this parliament refused to incorporate any more life insurance companies and decided that the operations of existing ones were to be examined thoroughly as to the effects on the Canadian economy of the disposition of the savings of the Canadian people in the hands of life insurance companies, we might have a basis for deciding just how we are to handle this key factor in economic development and progress.
I have suggested before and I suggest again that we took a slight step in this direction when we developed the Canada Pension Plan. In fact, I recall that at that time there were some wails from life insurance companies that were already beginning to feel the effects on their businesses of the coverage provided by the Canada Pension Plan. This cheered me up immensely. I thought: Obviously this is the way in which to deal with this problem.
I would not for a moment suggest that we should attempt to expropriate private life insurance companies. No one in his right senses would want to expropriate a whole raft of insurance agents. But I suggest that we should offer the Canadian people another and a better way of disposing of their savings than turning them over to private institutions. I can see that if the Canada Pension Plan were expanded to include options comparable with the options provided by private life insurance companies, something over $1 billion a year which now goes into life insurance premiums would come into the hands of the public authority. I would have thought the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) would seize very quickly on this idea, considering that he has had so many difficulties lately. Here would be a source of the funds that the government requires. They could be well protected by government bonds. This money could be made available for the sort of programs upon which this and any future government will have to embark.
[DOT] (6:10 p.m.)
But before doing so I would again urge that we examine the alternative, which is to continue this business of incorporating anything up to a dozen new life insurance companies in
Private Bills
every session of parliament. To my mind this is utter nonsense. It is not as though we were expanding the pool of Canadian savings but rather that we are licensing small fishermen to fish in it. It is the same pool. We are fragmenting it into sections which are difficult to control. It is very difficult to determine what the final disposition of these funds will be. I would hope that the government and parliament will take this seriously under consideration.
There is a very strong tendency today in other fields of insurance to move out of the private field. Hospital insurance used to be dominated by private insurance companies. We now have our hospital bills covered by various public methods, depending on what province we come from. In my own province hospital costs are paid out of the consolidated revenue. When the government finally, if it ever does, gets around to the implementation of the medicare bill, much of the insurance business which was devoted to providing medical care will also pass into the public sector. There has been a continuing demand, of course, all across the country for the public authority to take over the insurance of automobiles because of the tremendous charges made by insurance companies for that type of insurance. But even more important than these is the question of life insurance savings because by and large these are a proportion of income which people set aside for their old age, to ensure the education of their children, and to ensure some economic and financial stability for the family. This should be the concern of the public authority, and I and my colleagues will continue stressing this every time one of these private life insurance bills comes before the house.
I know it may seem unfair that we should deal with those companies which stick their heads up here in this chamber and not do anything about the ones which never appear before us because they are already well established. But I am sure hon. members will have realized from what I have said that we do not consider blocking these bills as anything more than a preliminary step toward a complete review of what, as I said, is a chaotic situation in the handling of the savings of Canadian people. I hope that parliament will finally impress upon private individuals and members of the house the undesirability of bringing any more of these bills before the house until we have made a complete examination of the operations of life insurance companies and the part they play
