in the development of our economy in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, once more we have before us the proposal of the Excelsior Life Insurance Company to become a federal company rather than a provincially incorporated one. That in itself raises some interesting questions about the whole subject of the operation of insurance companies. My colleague, the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Cameron), has just made the suggestion that perhaps some form of inquiry into this matter might be instituted. He even went so far as to suggest that perhaps a commission of inquiry might be established. I believe that this bill and the principle contained in the explanatory note bring out very well one of the areas which such a commission of inquiry might explore. I refer to the rather strange practice under our federal system of government of companies being incorporated provincially and then seeking to transmogrify themselves into another form of corporate being. As the superintendent of insurance pointed out when a bill identical to this one was before the standing committee of the house in an earlier session, this is a somewhat different process than that normally followed in such a change.
If the argument advanced by the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands, which I and other hon. members have advanced from time to time in connection with certain other bills, about the impact of the operation of insurance companies on the direction of investment of the pool of savings of the Canadian people is a valid one, and if one looks at the volume of business transacted by insurance companies, it should become apparent to all hon. members that this process is an important factor in influencing the direction in which our economy moves or does not move at the present time. I think one must agree that companies which establish themselves under the authority of a provincial legislature usually operate in that way for a while and then move into the field of a federally incorporated company. This is an important question which needs examination.
We hear a good deal these days about the problems facing the Minister of Finance and the government of Canada in exercising effective monetary and fiscal controls in the operation of the economy. Much has been said about the dangers which exist when the economy becomes overheated or suddenly becomes underheated. All these questions are definitely tied in with the kind of proposal

which in this instance is made by the Excelsior Life Insurance Company.
As is pointed out in the explanatory note, the company has been established in Canada for a long time. It was incorporated by letters patent dated August 7, 1889, in the province of Ontario, and it is one of several provincial life insurance companies registered with the federal department of insurance under part IX of the Canadian and British Insurance Companies Act. The note goes on to point out the differences between the provincial and federal legislation in respect of the operation of insurance companies.
This brief explanation of the reason for the desire of the company to change its incorporation, which is the principle of the bill before us, was expanded on by Mr. Hum-phrys before the standing committee of the house on Tuesday, February 14, 1967. After having pointed out that the company was incorporated in 1889 by letters patent in Ontario, he went on to say:
Since 1897-
Not long after it first began its operations.
-it has been registered under the federal insurance laws and has been supervised by the federal insurance department, but as a provincial company. Therefore it had its powers under provincial legislation, but it had voluntarily made itself subject to the federal insurance acts and the supervision of the federal insurance department.
He went on to point out that the federal insurance act imposed certain restrictions on it and that in some instances acceptance of the federal rules has in his view created certain difficulties for this company from which companies incorporated directly by federal law did not suffer.
[DOT] (6:20 p.m.)
I suppose the proponent of the passage of this bill would argue that this inconvenience to the company should be removed without question at their request. However, so far as I am concerned the testimony opens up some rather important aspects, not only in relation to the general economic life of the country but the constitutional situation in which we find ourselves. We all know that a federal-provincial constitutional conference is to convene here shortly. We are aware that the conference will concern itself more with such matters as individual human rights; perhaps I should say with matters of the spirit rather than the flesh. Nevertheless, the fact that we are on the eve of what has been hailed as a very important federal-provincial conference on the future of our constitution brings to
February 1, 1968

mind many important areas which need to be considered but which are not in the agenda of the conference. These matters might well be considered further as we seek to develop a new constitution, if that is what we are seeking to achieve, for the operation of Canada as a federal state.
The complexities and difficulties in respect of this company raise in my mind certain questions about whether the present arrangement, which allows insurance companies to incorporate either federally or provincially and to operate under a hodge-podge of different laws and regulations, is desirable or is in the economic interests of Canadians generally. This kind of question might very well be examined by a board of inquiry with broad powers. Such a board could also get the views of provincial authorities who have had experience in dealing with insurance companies in their own jurisdictions. If we are going to have a more orderly direction of the flow of investment funds in this country in the future than we have had in the past, it seems to me there are obvious advantages to some kind of uniform legislation covering these companies. This would seem to be the case as long as we have private insurance companies operating in the country, and I expect that will be for a good many years yet. We should not leave it to the whim or fancy of a particular firm such as Excelsior Life to decide whether or not it wishes to operate under an Ontario charter or a federal charter.
This company, according to the evidence given by the superintendent of insurance, is one of the major companies in Canada, even though apparently it is not controlled in Canada. I can see some merit in such a company being governed by federal insurance laws and supervised by the federal insurance department. As Mr. Humphrys points out, the proposal by this company that it be changed to a federal company is purely voluntary on its part. Apparently the company has operated quite successfully since 1897 under the present arrangement.
This opens up the whole question of whether or not this kind of arrangement should be left to the voluntary action of the company or whether it is the type of thing that should be dealt with in a more orderly and rational manner through some such means as a special commission of inquiry. Such a commission would have powers beyond those of a parliamentary committee inasmuch as it would be able to spend more time and engage the necessary help to get evidence and opinions
Private Bills
from provincial authorities. I hope, Mr. Speaker, that these ideas will receive consideration.
A large organization such as Excelsior Life obviously has not suffered too seriously from the existing disability. If this situation were left as it is until the matter can be decided in a broader way than by the simple adoption of this bill, that might be a more desirable course of action. If any temporary inconvenience of a minor nature, which apparently the company has experienced from time to time, should continue for a further period this would not seriously affect the operations of the company and might very well be more in keeping with the real interests of the Canadian people than the simple adoption of this bill by parliament.
There are many other issues inherent in this bill, just as there have been in some of the other proposals made by insurance companies in bills which have been coming before the house. One question which has received a lot of attention in parliament and in the country in recent years has been interest rates. Mention is made in the evidence given about this company that at one point there was a difference between the federal insurance laws and the Ontario law with regard to the amount an insurance company could invest in mortgages.
It was pointed out that in 1965 the federal insurance law was amended to permit companies investing in mortgages to lend up to 75 per cent of the value of the property, whereas formerly it was two thirds. At the time the federal law was changed the Ontario legislation still imposed a limit of two-thirds on insurance companies incorporated within that province. It was pointed out that while federally incorporated companies could then use the 75 per cent formula, this company was still restricted because of its provincial charter to two-thirds. I suggest this situation raises the whole issue of the direction of mortgage funds into various areas of mortgage activity. Since Excelsior is a large company it probably has directed a large pool of funds into mortgage activity.
We have heard a lot of discussion about the availability of mortgage funds for certain purposes. We recognize that the pool of these funds is only a certain size. The Minister of Labour (Mr. Nicholson), as spokesman for Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, and more recently the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Benson), have made various proposals to cope with this problem. By and

February 1. 1968

large, the only answer given by the government has been that the ceiling on interest rates must be removed so that mortgage funds can be attracted into housebuilding. Who decides where investment funds are to go? Those funds go to the kind of companies with which we deal in these private bills. According to this bill, Excelsior Life Insurance Company is one company that is interested in using its funds for mortgage purposes.
[DOT] (6:30 p.m.)
It seems to me obvious that in dealing with these bills we have, in effect, been helping to aggravate the problems that the minister who reports to parliament on housing has had to face. On the admission of various spokesmen for the government from time to time, the problem has been that bodies such as Excelsior Life have been directing their mortgage funds, at their whim and fancy, into fields other than housing, because at a given point in time they seemed to find them more lucrative for investment purposes. I think Excelsior Life would be different from some of the other insurance companies, if it had not directed some of its mortgage funds into the erection of large office buildings, or possibly shopping centres which it is suggested from time to time are somewhat redundant in relation to the real need of the present day for adequate housing for our people.
If Excelsior Life feels that there is some hesitancy on our part to transform them into a federal company by means of a rather strange legislative enactment in order, so it is suggested, to make it a little simpler for the company to change their corporate status and thus remove this little inconvenience, then let the company take note of the fact that some of us are concerned about the right of bodies such as this to decide, in effect, whether or not the Canadian people are going to have sufficient housing.
I suggest that these are the kinds of issues that are involved in the bills with which we deal during this hour. The other day I was speaking on another bill, and I said there are some of us who are not prepared simply to agree that the convenience of any particular company, whether Excelsior Life or some other, should take precedence over action which, in our view, should be taken to meet the real interests of the Canadian people whom we in this parliament are elected to represent. So I have no hesitation in saying that this particular proposal is not one which we should pass lightly.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I must interrupt the hon. member to inform him that his time has expired.

Mr. Speaker, in commenting on Bill S-8 that is before the house this evening, I would point out that the Senate banking and commerce committee heard evidence from the proponents of the bill which indicated that the purpose of the bill was to convert a provincially incorporated company into a federal corporation. This would not make too much difference to the operations of the company; in fact, it would only enhance its prestige in the community.
The evidence presented to the committee on banking and commerce revealed one fact that I should like to draw to the attention of this house. Under questioning it was revealed that the major share interest in the company is owned by a United States company, the Aetna Life Insurance Company. The major interest, about 70 per cent, was acquired in 1960. I am quite surprised that this acquisition was made at such late date. We all know from the pronouncement of the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) that the government is endeavouring to gain control of the Canadian economy, eventually wresting it from the hands of foreign nations. Certainly this particular move at a date as late as 1960 is not in accordance with stated government policy.
Different government.

No matter whether it was a different government, I have stated on many occasions that I do not see much difference between the actions of those who form the government and those who form the opposition. The same trend appears to be continuing. Companies have changed hands time and time again over the last 100 years but the trend toward foreign ownership has gradually increased. Regardless of who was in power, I know of no time when this trend has reversed itself, enabling Canadians to gain control of their own economy.
In order to get to the root of the trouble, Mr. Speaker, and to understand the insurance business in Canada, I should like to delve into the reason insurance companies exist and to relate to the house what motivates people to buy insurance. It is surprising to me that in this affluent nation of ours there should be so much fear of economic disaster as a result of death that the people of Canada should see fit to put so much money into insurance. It is also a condemnation of past governments that
February 1, 1968

the people of this country live in such fear that they have to protect their dependants from economic disaster as a result of death.
Statistics show that the level of insurance has increased five times over the figure for 1950. It has increased twice as fast as incomes have increased. Why is this, Mr. Speaker? It is because the people of Canada have not been provided with a sense of security by past administrations. Who are the people buying insurance, Mr. Speaker? You would think that the man with spare money in his pocket would invest in insurance. However, statistics show that this is not the case. They reveal that 50 per cent of life insurance policies are bought by people with $5,000 income or less; and 83 per cent of all life insurance in Canada is bought by people who earn less than $7,500. This shows that there is fear, that the small wage earner is in fear of not being able to provide for his family and he must take advantage of this type of protection.
Over 93 per cent of the Canadian people carry life insurance and 83 per cent of those who buy that insurance are in the under $7,500 a year income bracket. You can see that the little man carries the life insurance companies on his back. I think that the government should provide some sort of security for our people so that those who live in desperate fear will not need to go to private insurance companies to relieve their minds in order to sleep more soundly at night.
[DOT] (6:40 p.m.)
One of my colleagues has said that the government sponsored insurance plan would have been twice as good had there not been interference by the private insurance companies, which realize what will happen to them if the government proceeds to expand plans like the Canada Pension Plan. The introduction of the Canada Pension Plan and Quebec pension plan reduced the group annuity payments to private insurance companies by 14 per cent. One piece of legislation transferred to the public sector 14 per cent of the premiums that had been paid to the private sector. Since in one year that amounts to about $1,300 million, one can see that a sizeable amount of money is involved, and that money can be directed by the government toward the best needs of the people.
A great public lobby is being conducted by various organizations which want to show that the foreign insurance companies operating in this country are good corporate citizens. "Good corporate citizen" is an expression that has been coined by insurance
Private Bills
associations, manufacturers associations and Chambers of Commerce, the inference being that a corporation is almost human, with flesh and bones. It is not. A corporation is made of bricks, bank books and bank accounts. It has no blood and bones. The terms "corporate responsibility", "good corporation citizenship" and others like them are cliches.
During housing debates in this house some hon. members have said that mortgage funds are in short supply in those areas that most need them. Since most of our mortgage funds are tied up in insurance companies, those companies have the power practically to direct this country and to tell it where the money is to be invested. We know that insurance companies do not invest in the mari-times, and that the maritimes need investment money perhaps more than other areas of Canada need it. We cannot control the insurance companies in their investing.
Foreign owned insurance companies have not complied with the wishes of the Prime Minister, and I support him in that regard, even though the government has not done much, actively, to reduce the number of foreign owned insurance companies operating in this country.
In 1966, speaking only of life insurance companies and excluding those companies which sell fire, automobile and health insurance as well as other types, there were in Canada 116 companies which sold life insurance. Forty one of those were Canadian and 75 were foreign. Since the 75 foreign owned companies probably do more business than the 41 Canadian companies, most of our premium dollars were controlled by foreigners.
It is strange to find British and United States companies operating in Canada while no United States company operates in the British Isles and no British company operates in the United States. I do not know what the saw-off was, but that is how things are. In Canada, life insurance is sold by United States, British, Netherlands, Swiss, German and French companies. We seem to have no control over who comes in and takes our premium dollar. In the United States they seem to have some control, and in the British Isles they have some control. We, on the other hand, let five or six different nations come in with their insurance companies, and we let those companies control about 60 per cent of our insurance business.
I was interested in a speech given by Mr. W. W. Foot, president and general manager of

Economical Mutual Insurance Company of Kitchener, as reported in the Globe and Mail. Mr. Foot, being critical of newspaper reporters and editors, is reported to have said: Reporters and editors are involved in a conspiracy with governments to promote nationalization of the general insurance business.
I do not know whether government members are conspiring with the newspaper people. That is for the government members to answer. Mr. Foot was critical not only of newspapermen but of his own colleagues as well:
The insurance industry... at one time extols the virtue of free enterprise competition and simultaneously takes measures to promote uniformity of operation.
He goes on to say:
Competition is cut-throat, unbridled, always vicious. Among ourselves, inwardly, we abhor competition. If a company, through its management, conforms to the uniform standards promulgated by the Establishment, agents are disposed to look upon it as a stick-in-the-mud, but when it adopts any form of deviation from the standards of the Establishment, everyone shouts "Stop rocking the boat".
This is a sort of admission that there is price fixing, that a cartel agreement to fix rates is in effect. He goes on to say:
Consider our practice of announcing rate increases in the press each year... By so doing we invite criticism; we create the image of a monopoly.
Usually we see a blanket increase in automobile or other insurance rates. Each company will charge an increase across the board, and yet each company will claim to be engaged in free enterprise. To my way of thinking, they are all monopoly oriented.
In order to grant members of this house more time to consider this bill, Mr. Speaker, I move seconded by the hon. member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Fawcett):
That this bill be not now read the second time but that it be read a second time this day six months hence.

speechtext: Is the house ready for the question?
Question.

Mr. Speaker, I regret that my friends in the N.D.P. have taken this opportunity to mount their campaign against the insurance industry. I think they have picked the wrong victim.

As has been admitted by many speakers of that party who always dominate these discussions, this is an old established Canadian company which simply seeks to clear up the confusion about its status in a way which the superintendent of insurance entirely approved in the hearings on a similar bill which were held before the miscellaneous private bills committee during the last session.
[DOT] (6:50 p.m.)
I will resist the temptation to answer the many arguments which were put forward by spokesmen for the New Democratic party and which pertained to this company-there were many others which had nothing to do with the company or with the bill now before us. I will simply suggest that there is much merit in the words of the superintendent of insurance when he appeared before the standing committee on miscellaneous private bills on February 14, 1967. I quote his statement as it appears on page 60 of the minutes of proceedings and evidence, No. 4.
I think by moving over and subjecting itself more firmly to federal jurisdiction and really cutting off all the provincial control and authority, it is clearing up an uncertainty and untidiness of its present position. If at some future date parliament decides that it will impose a more severe policy on foreign ownership, this company will be affected by it, but if we leave this company as it is, it will not be.
Hon. members opposite are defeating the purpose of their present campaign by picking on this particular bill as a convenient vehicle for the expression of their idea that there should be no new life insurance companies in Canada. This is not a new company: It is a well-established company which seems to be highly respected. The bill before the house is one which has been approved by all the government agencies concerned, and was recommended during the committee hearing last session by the superintendent of insurance. I appeal to the house to defeat the motion.

The house resumed from Thursday, November 23,	1967 consideration of the
motion of Mr. Cameron (High Park) for the second reading of Bill No. C-112, to incorporate Aetna Casualty Company of Canada, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Gilbert (p. 1746).

This bill is somewhat different in its nature from the one about which I was speaking a few minutes ago. This is an insurance company to insure virtually everything but life. In clause 6 we find a list of 26 types of coverage running the whole gamut of possible disasters including fire insurance, accident insurance, aircraft insurance, automobile insurance, boiler insurance, credit insurance, earthquake insurance, explosion insurance', falling aircraft insurance, forgery insurance, guarantee insurance, hail insurance, impact by vehicle insurance, plate glass insurance, sickness insurance, sprinkler leakage insurance, weather insurance and windstorm insurance. It is perhaps a good thing we have only 26 letters in the alphabet.
Again, Mr. Speaker, I believe we should be considering whether all these forms of insurance ought to be in private hands. As I was saying some time ago, there is a widespread demand for automobile insurance to be taken out of private hands because of the way in which private companies have handled this necessary feature of modern life. The same could be said of other areas in which insurance companies engage in business.
This bill proposes to incorporate a company which is, I believe, largely owned outside the country. I do not know whether that is very important, one way or another. I object to private individuals engaging in this sort of business, whether Canadian or not. There are some who become very agitated if they see that ventures of this kind are foreign-owned and I suppose that if we are to have people battening on the economy we should confine this privilege to Canadians.
My suggestion is that government and this parliament should subject such undertakings to careful scrutiny. Are we not moving into a
Private Bills
new era in which many of the things once carried out by private companies should be carried out by a public authority which would provide coverage at minimum cost?
There is no question but that the proliferation of companies in the insurance field must add to the cost of the services provided. Some people may question this, but I can assure them that it costs twice as much to hire two men as it does to hire one. The more insurance companies there are, the more people will have to make a living out of them. Consequently, the cost to the insured person is bound to continue to rise.
May I call it seven o'clock?

speechtext: Order. When the committee rose at six o'clock subclause (h) was being considered, with an amendment by the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona.

Mr. Chairman, when the house proceeded to private members business a little over two and a half hours ago I had been discussing some of the comments that had been made by members of the government on the position that our party has taken in the debate on this subclause, and on the position which members on the government side feel has been manifested by their own colleagues on the government benches. Needless to say there is a wide divergence of opinion between us on this side and the spokesmen to whom I refer on the other side with regard to the sincerity of the position purportedly taken by members on the government side. I was referring to the remarks made by the hon. member for York-Scarborough in which he alleged and purported to suggest that there was division in my party with regard to subclause (h), and that by contrast there was remarkable unanimity and community of thought and purpose among the members on the government benches. I asked the hon. member for York-Scarborough, in a rhetorical way perhaps, just where he would place such members of his party as the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo, the hon. member for York-Humber, the hon. member for Coast-Capilano, the hon. member for St. Paul's, and the hon. member for Spadina. Indeed I could go on naming hon. members. The five hon. members who I have named have hardly risen in this chamber to profess a deep philosophical and sincere commitment to the position of the government on this subclause. On the contrary, both inside and outside this chamber, some of them at least have given every evidence that they are as much opposed to the principle contained in subclause (h) as we in this party are. I must say that the difference of posture between these members and the members of our party has been very evident when the crunch came and the votes were taken, because many of them have
DEBATES	6275
Canadian Policy on Broadcasting absented themselves from the chamber so as not to have to participate in them. Those of us, however, who have taken the philosophical position which I and many others in my party have enunciated in the past week have been here to participate in these votes, and we have put our political money where our principles and our philosophical beliefs are. [DOT] (8:40 p.m.)
Although the hon. member for York-Scarborough made a very urbane and intelligent speech and, in his usual poised political manner, exposed what he considered to be the essence of the argument, I suggest he was treading on dangerous ground. He cannot, in all conscience, support the argument that his party is united philosophically on this question and is the only party in this house to be so united when his colleagues have stood in this chamber during the last 72 hours and proposed amendments which would, in effect, substantially change the wording of the subclause in question. These amendments would have put the subclause in line with the philosophical expression to which we adhere in this house. I cannot explain the absence of those hon. members when votes on such amendments have taken place. This is something which the hon. member for York-Scarborough will have to settle with his own conscience.
Both the member for York-Scarborough and the hon. member for Verdun have made emotional appeals for some leadership, some direction from the head of this party in so far as this particular dispute is concerned. I suggest that this is a specious appeal to make in this chamber. There is absolutely no reason why members of this party or of any party in this house should not, when we are examining legislation of this kind clause by clause, speak out and state their individual convictions, and suggest their individual, independent points of view. The difference is, of course, that those of us who form this party have for a long time, certainly throughout our political lives, adhered to the tradition of independence and freedom which is part and parcel of the philosophy of Conservativism. Obviously members on the other side of the chamber are muzzled and the verbal expression certain members may wish to make of their convictions is denied them. There are handcuffs on those same members so far as any overt action is concerned.
We are at a stage in studying this legislation where every one of the 265 members

Canadian Policy on Broadcasting should, in accordance with parliamentary tradition and devotion to the democratic political principles oi this country, stand and make his or her own, individual, independent views known on the parts of this legislation with which there is not agreement. There is absolutely no reason why there should be a crystallization of the position of this party on this legislation at this stage, either by the leader of this party or anyone acting on his behalf. When it comes to leadership, sir, I suggest that those on the other side of the chamber are treading on very dangerous ground. If they asked members on this side of the chamber if they felt the Liberal party had provided this country with the type of leadership Canadians have been crying for during the last four years, the answer would be a resounding no.
When members opposite talk about leadership, they should first put their own house in order. If there had been leadership provided on this broadcasting question, none of the explosions of the past two years in the field of broadcasting would have occurred. They have asked, Mr. Chairman, where we stand in this party on this particular philosophical question. I think it has been made clear where we stand, where the consensus in the party lies. Where members have different points of view, as I have attempted to suggest, it is incumbent upon them at this stage in the study of the legislation to express those different, independent points of view.
The hon. member for York-Scarborough has attended faithfully throughout the tedious hours of this debate and is familiar with the stand of this party on this philosophical question. He has been here throughout the week when the consensus on that philosophical point has developed and been articulated by this party. His answer lies in the Hansard record for the past four days.
I was mildly distressed, Mr. Chairman, by a reference the minister made, really outside the area of debate, which seemed to suggest to me that she felt such members as the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo and I have an axe to grind in this debate, since we have spent some time in the field of private broadcasting. I submit to the hon. lady that she has cast unfair aspersions upon both the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo and me. I believe these allegations are unsupportable. If she checks my remarks during this debate, in fact if she goes back to my speech on first reading in this house and the meetings in the standing committee, she will see that I have tried to

emphasize the fact that I am not speaking in defence of, nor am I particularly interested in, the objectives or aims of private broadcasting any more than I am in the objectives and aims of publicly owned broadcasting. What I am talking about, the element in which I am interested-and I thought I had made it perfectly clear in my remarks-is the viewing and listening public. I am interested in the right of that public to have its objectives, its ambitions and interests preserved and paramount when any conflict arises between the two elements of our Canadian broadcasting system. There has been no attempt on my part, and I think the same can be said for the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo, to expostulate the position of private broadcasters. Hers is not a true charge.
The position I have taken, and that the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo certainly took in very articulate fashion in the standing committee, so far as this clause was concerned was that it was the public interest that should be paramount. It is the public interest which is the only justifiable criterion in this dispute. It is the public interest that is abrogated and violated in the wording of the subclause as it was originally constituted, and as it is now constituted in amended form.
Members on the government side may wonder why I took the particular voting position I took yesterday when we had an amendment which subsequently passed, but to which the member for Okanagan-Revelstoke moved a subamendment. The subamendment, if it had been carried, would have accomplished the same thing as my original amendment moved on Tuesday of this week. I did not support the subamendment moved by the hon. member for Okanagan-Revelstoke, although I agreed with it 100 per cent, because my colleague, the member for Halifax, had an amendment which would have been completely neutralized by the passage of the subamendment. I did not vote on that issue. I neither voted for the subamendment nor against it. I voted against the amendment of the hon. member for Halifax purely on the grounds that I had to be able to justify the remarks which I would make subsequently, and which I am making now. I felt I could not justify a further intervention in the debate if I voted for the amendment. I submit this argument to hon. members as my rationalization of my voting position of yesterday on the subamendment and the amendment before the committee.

I was exercised to a degree also, Mr. Chairman, by the remarks made earlier today in the chamber by the hon. member for Burna-by-Richmond. Before we even reached this aspect of the debate the hon. member said that the N.D.P. would be against any change in the amended paragraph (h). He said: "We"-meaning his party-"supported the original subclause and we supported the amendment moved yesterday by the member of the official opposition"-the hon. member for Halifax. He also said that he and his group would be against any further change in the clause.
[DOT] (8:50 p.m.)
That hardly came as surprising news to any of us. Of course he would be against it, because the amended clause says precisely what the original clause said. That is our objection to the amendment. The hon. member was originally opposed to any change to paragraph (h). Therefore when an amendment is moved that is precisely the same, with the exception that it moves the emphasis further down in the sentence by changing the phrasing but does not change the essence of the paragraph, he would naturally be in favour of the amendment and opposed to any amendment that we might suggest to soften or modify the rigid position enunciated in the paragraph.
I also felt that his subsequent references to filibustering on the part of members of this house were unworthy of him. The hon. member has contributed greatly to the formulation of this broadcasting policy and the creation of the bill before us. I do not want to engage in argument with him over allegations that either he or I might make against each other's respective parties and positions, but considering the high level of intelligence and conscientiousness that he has brought to the debate I did feel that that remark was beneath him. There has been no filibustering by anyone in this party. We are concerned about the serious oversight in the wording of this legislation which compromises the most important element in Canadian society-the public interest.
If some of us missed things in the early examination of this legislation, then we are sorry and apologize. It is not always possible to come quickly to a satisfactory understanding of every clause in every piece of legislation with which we in this chamber are confronted. Sometimes re-examination and a period of contemplation is required before one comes to, as it were, the moment of 27053-396j

Canadian Policy on Broadcasting truth in respect to a particular phrase or provision. Only then is the weakness or strength of that particular part of the legislation properly focused before us. That is what may have happened as far as some members on this side of the chamber are concerned.
In my own heart and conscience I can fully justify and defend the position that I have taken in this debate. In no way should the stand I have taken be construed as a filibuster. I have made a sincere attempt to change a piece of legislation in such a way as to protect the most important part of Canadian society-the Canadian interest. I have made a sincere attempt to soften and to modify wording which to me smacks of stateism, authoritarianism, and which to say the least is discriminatory. It is not a question of its being discriminatory in respect of private broadcasters but of its being discriminatory in respect of, if you like, private enterprise, discriminatory in respect of the independent, free-thinking, free-moving Canadian.
I cannot understand why the minister has been so intractable on this point. I was dismayed, to say the least, when the amendment I moved earlier this afternoon failed to find favour with the minister. I felt it satisfied both philosophical positions in this debate without watering down the position of the government. It satisfied the concern on this side of the chamber for free enterprise and the public interest and in no way represented a defeat, moral or otherwise, for anyone participating in this debate.
Disappointed as I was, even more than that I was amazed that the minister found the wording of my amendment so unacceptable. For my own part I find the wording of the paragraph as it now stands completely repugnant from a philosophical point of view. I see no justification whatever for it and I certainly support the amendment that has been moved at this point in the debate by my colleague from Edmonton-Strathcona.
I would be interested to hear the minister or some of her colleagues defend the clause as it now stands and explain why the term "public interest" has throughout the debate seemed to be so reprehensible to the government. It was through the efforts of this party that this term was put into that particular paragraph. The original paragraph made no reference to it. However, the clause is not yet satisfactory to us, even though that term is in the paragraph. To put it there we have had an uphill struggle against ministerial intransigence.
6278	COMMONS
Canadian Policy on Broadcasting
Why is the minister so loath to write into the legislation something that is in the best traditions of Canadian democracy and which should be in the best traditions of the Liberal party, the protection and primacy of the public interest? One is quickly persuaded to come to the conclusion, as did the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings two nights ago in this chamber, that this debate has separated the champions of individualism and independence from that sparkless, faceless army of people who would see this country complete its alarming slide into state-ism, socialism and total welfare-ism.
From that, one is logically forced to the conclusion that we are one of the few countries that seems to be stubbornly and unwisely bucking a political and philosophical trend in the world. Countries like Denmark are getting away from the totally socialistic, authoritarian concept of government, while countries that still stick with it, such as Great Britain, are suffering the slings and arrows of the most outrageous social, political and economic fortunes.
This lesson is being written in every corner of the western world, yet this country seems to go on stubbornly resisting and ignoring it, plunging headlong down the path to welfare-ism, socialism and authoritarian control, sapping the society in which we live of all its ambition and robbing it of all its dreams.
[DOT] (9:00 p.m.)
I think the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings made the point most eloquently two days ago in his charge to the members on the government benches with respect to the choice facing them and the test ahead of them, as they go into their leadership convention. They must ask themselves, under whom will their party live? The tragedy, of course, is that the Canadian people are involved in this exercise. If it were a party choosing a leader for itself with no one else involved, it would be different. But here they are carrying out their exercise for the whole Canadian public, and what they do will affect the government of this country. In effect, they are choosing the direction that the government and the country will take. That is where the tragedy lies.
Before closing and yielding the floor, I hope, to my colleague from Edmonton-Strath-cona, who intends to speak further on his amendment, I ask again, as I have asked on some five prior occasions in this debate, what are the objectives of the national broadcasting service? If I thought that the objectives

DEBATES	February 1, 1968
were clearly enunciated and did not encroach on the individual rights of individual, free Canadians, did not encroach on the civil liberties of Canadian men and women, I might subscribe, I dare say, to the clause as it originally stood or in its amended form.
But I am not satisfied that the objectives of the national broadcasting service have been properly defined in this bill and I appeal once again to the minister, in the interests of liberalism, socialism, conservatism and every other ism in the spectrum of Canadian politics, in the interests of Canada and the Canadian tradition of freedom and enterprise, to yield on this one point, to satisfy a great many people inside and outside the broadcasting industry who, I can assure her, are concerned with the apparent authoritarianism of amended subclause (h) and with the apparent, arbitrary and permanent conclusion that broadcasting authorities are charged to reach where conflicts in broadcasting arise in future between the public and private sectors of the industry-that is, between the national broadcasting service and the private part of the system.
The subclause means that a decision has been reached that will guide the authorities for all time. The scales are to be weighted and the jury shall be directed to find in favour of the national broadcasting service. The case of the private individual and of the public, and after all it is the public that is most concerned in this matter, is compromised, foreshortened and doomed to failure before the litigation has begun.

On reading the bill, it became apparent that if the interest of the national broadcasting service in any matter were but one per cent and the interest of private broadcasters were 99 per cent, a decision would have to be rendered in favour of the national broadcasting service. But this clause went too far, and the object of the hon. member was to try to obtain agreement to amendments that would ameliorate that provision and let us get on with the business of the house.
The difficulty, Mr. Chairman, was that the wording was arrived at hastily round about noon. The minister took a look at it, said she would accept it, and we went back to the house without anybody having had a chance to study the amendment. When it was read to us it revealed words which said that the matter shall be resolved in the public interest, and so on, and the thought came to me that that was not what was in mind. The language of the subclause would be that in case of conflict the matter would be resolved in the public interest; but I submit that the suggestion is that when there is no conflict, a decision in favour of the national broadcasting service is not in the public interest. In other words, we seem to be directing someone to do something that is not in the public interest.

It was my hope that by drawing attention to this situation, a poor choice of words in an amendment which had been drafted hastily in an honest endeavour by the minister to meet the feeling by hon. members on this side of the house as well as, I believe, on her own side of the house, the minister would become aware of what had happened and would be agreeable to finding another form of words which would meet the case. Mr. Speaker, I notice that the Postmaster General is present and in his place. I welcome this opportunity to deal with what is essentially a grievance that is felt by a majority of the residents of the village of Libau, Manitoba. Unfortunately there is insufficient time to detail with precision the sequence of events and the timing that lay behind the decision of the Postmaster General to transfer the post office and postmastership at Libau last November, but the Postmaster General is
DEBATES	6285
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion well aware that his course of action was found to be very unsatisfactory. The people there took the opportunity to petition him not once but on two occasions, asking him to give consideration to their complaints, their allegations and their request to make an order to retransfer the post office and postmastership back to its location prior to last November. The complaint that the people make is that the minister did not act fairly in that not enough time was given between the issuance of the order of transfer and the date when the actual transfer was to take effect. In fact, I calculate that only four working days were allowed to elapse between notice of transfer and the actual transfer itself.
I must say that the minister was good enough to request or to order a delay in this transfer, during which time-a period of three or four weeks-he considered the request of the residents of this district. However, I and the people of Libau are not satisfied that he was able to justify or sufficiently explain why it was necessary to make this transfer.
The minister has told them in letters, and has told me in the house, that the main reason this transfer was made was that the store in which this post office was located had in recent years changed hands too frequently, and that therefore there was an element of instability. According to the first news reports that carried this announcement, the minister stated that the store in which the post office was located had changed hands three times in four years. This was later amended to three times in five years. I can state with complete accuracy that it changed hands three times in 19 years.
Not only that, Mr. Speaker, but the people of Libau cannot understand why it was found necessary to transfer the post office, in view of the fact that the postmaster who held the position prior to last November had held it for a period of four months or so and his work was found to be satisfactory. In fact I have a letter showing that the regional director of postal services in Winnipeg found the performance of the former postmaster to be quite satisfactory.
[DOT] (10:10 p.m.)
In light of that it is difficult to understand why the minister did as he did. When the overwhelming majority of the people make a request, and when what they request will not complicate the minister's job, I submit that that request ought to be acceded to. What was

6286	COMMONS
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion requested would not have affected national policy and I fail to understand why it was not granted.
The people have petitioned twice for the return of the post office. Had the minister granted that request, would that have affected the operation of his department and the rest of the country? Would it have increased the expenditure of public funds? The answer is that it would not. There was therefore no substantial reason for the minister's refusal.
The request was made and the petition was signed by 75 per cent of the adult residents of the district. In one of his recent letters the minister challenges the accuracy of that figure and suggests that the percentage is more like 67 per cent. But 67 per cent in favour indicates an overwhelming majority. While perhaps I should not challenge the minister's figure, I do so, because the official list of postal subscribers is wrong. Mr. Speaker, I know that I do not have much time to answer, but I shall try to be as brief as possible.
First of all, there is some misunderstanding about the word "transfer". A post office in that class is not transferred, any more than a postmaster is transferred. The appointee must provide the premises himself. This does not mean, therefore, that when a postmaster resigns, either because he sells his business or for some other reason, the post office must remain in the same premises. What we do is that we appoint a new local postmaster who must provide his own premises.
The business has been sold three times since 1962. The hon. member knows that did not cost the department anything but each


time the postmaster resigns or is transferred, the civil servants of the department must go to the post office and take an inventory of the stamps, money orders, etc. and see that everything is in order. This, of course, entails new expenses.
Because the new owner of the business, Mr. Gilson, was never appointed postmaster, the last postmaster, Mr. Greening, was appointed on a temporary basis, until such time as a permanent one is appointed. So, in this case, two people filled out applications, that is Messrs. Greening and Gilson. Of the two candidates, we have decided, with the assistance of the district manager in Winnipeg, that Mr. Greening was better qualified to fill the post. So I have agreed to make this appointment.
Now, even if a petition has been signed by many users of the mail, I must say that, today, 128 families out of 179 get their mail through the Libau post office. In all justice, Mr. Speaker, I surely cannot fire a postmaster who does his work adequately. I have never done that since I am Postmaster General and I will not do it because, in all justice, I think we should respect the persons on the job.
It may be that there was a misunderstanding when the question of transfer was brought up since, as I said earlier, the postmaster who was there had been hired only on a temporary basis, because the resignation of the one who sold the store had been received too late to appoint his successor.

welcome this opportunity to enlarge upon the question I put, or endeavoured to put, to the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Mcllraith) on January 26 in connection with federal construction in the city of Vancouver. Exceeding urgency attaches to this situation.
The shipbuilding industry is already facing a serious situation. One yard in Victoria is closed. Employment in the shipyard in Vancouver is down from 1,500 workers to fewer than 300. More than 60 per cent of the labour force dependant on this industry is unemployed and, according to the newspapers, in the course of only two days there were 500 inquiries by skilled workmen making application to go to the United States. This is the situation as it concerns shipbuilding.
We do not want to see a repetition of this situation in the general construction industry.
February 1, 1968

On January 15 I made a survey of the carpenters locals in Vancouver, New Westminster, Victoria and Nanaimo. I discovered that 22 per cent of the construction carpenters belonging to those four locals were unemployed. Unemployment among other construction workers such as electricians, plumbers, fitters and steel workers was similarly high.
Major construction work which has maintained employment during the past two years is coming to an end. No more pulp or paper mills are to be built in British Columbia in the foreseeable future. All the heavy power dam construction work on the Peace river and the Columbia river is approaching completion and no further major work is in sight for the next three years.
It is against this background, and bearing in mind the somewhat dismal outlook for the next two or three years, that I am asking the Minister of Public Works and the government whether they will not give favourable consideration to advancing the plan for the construction of the federal building to be built at the foot of Granville street. I know the government plans call for a start in 1970-71 on the first phase, 1973-74 on the second stage, and two or three years later on the third stage. In view of the factual situation and the unfortunate probable future for construction workers in Vancouver I just make the simple, and I think logical request that this one major federal project in Vancouver be planned and phased for an earlier start than 1970-71.

Mr. Speaker, we must recognize that this important project requires detailed negotiations which, if rushed through, cannot be carried out successfully. In addition, we must recognize that whether the building will be built by the Department of Public Works on the site now owned by the crown, or whether it will be built in some other way, the preparation of the plans and specifications will involve a great deal of work. These are the considerations that lead almost inevitably to the conclusion that the most realistic estimate that can be made at this time is that the construction phase of the work cannot be started within the next year or two.
I cannot comment on the accuracy of the hon. member's figures with regard to the unemployment situation. I will simply assume
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion that his figures are entirely accurate. Nevertheless, given the requirements for development of an arrangement and the development of plans and specifications, there seems to be no way in which this project can be moved ahead more rapidly.
I am not sure, Mr. Speaker, that it would be anything like the kind of solution to the employment problem that the hon. member suggests; but even if it were, I submit it would be almost totally impossible to put the construction into motion with anything like the kind of haste that he seems to have in mind.

On this occasion, Mr. Speaker, I shall be brief, unimpeded by my colleagues in my party. This is the day on which unification takes effect in the armed forces. Earlier today I presented the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Cadieux) with a question about the effect unification would have on the employment of prevailing rate people with the armed forces, and about what would happen to those who were laid off. It was a very short question. I hope my speech tonight will be short, and that the minister will be able to make his speech as long as he wishes so that the text of it can be sent forth to those people whose jobs may be in jeopardy.
I had a letter today from a particular branch of the armed forces in my area, concerning a number of men. One of them, an ex-serviceman, has served for 13 years, and another ex-serviceman has served for 16 years. There are three other people mentioned, one an ex-serviceman who has served for one and a half years, and two other prevailing rate employees without service, but who have served in one case for 15 years and in the other for two years.
Perhaps it is unfair to repeat gossip in this or any other place, but I have heard much gossip that there may be a rather drastic reduction in the complement of those who are classed as prevailing rate employees. Admittedly I have not been able to give the minister all the figures that have beset me, but I hope that in a general way he could give an indication to hon. members, which in turn they could send to prevailing rate employees, of what the future holds for them.

Mr. Speaker, I am very grateful to my hon. friend, the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. McCleave) for the conversation we had this afternoon on a particular subject. We are very sorry, we must admit, that there will be some reduction in the civilian staff as a result of our continuing efforts to bring about further improvements in the employment of our manpower resources within the department. Like everybody else, we face budget constraints. We are also streamlining our operation. We believe this is commendable.
It is regrettable that here and there some people, especially the casual workers, are
affected. I must point out, however, that we are making every effort to find suitable positions for those persons who have been or will be affected by the reorganization. In addition to our own internal efforts the officials of my department have written to the Department of Manpower and Immigration as well as the public service commission to solicit the collective efforts of the entire manpower organization in an effort to place the affected employees in other positions.
I can assure the hon. gentleman that all government departments are sparing no effort in their desire to assist these employees. I might also add that we give as much notice as is possible. In the case of the people the hon. member mentioned I believe three months notice was given. We are assisting in every way we can in order to help find suitable replacement employment for these people who eventually will lose or have lost their employment.
